The Fox jacopever (Sebastes vulpes) exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 8% [GSI = 8%] under the thermal conditions of its winter reproductive aggregation, at a water temperature of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]. Field collections made in the northwestern Pacific, particularly around the rocky reefs of southern Japan, suggest that this index remains stable across the early phases of the reproductive season. The gonadosomatic index was 8% [GSI = 8%], reflecting the cooler waters these fish typically inhabit at a temperature of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C].

Adult Fox jacopever reach a maximum total length of 43 cm [Li = 43 cm], a size that places this species among the medium-bodied members of the genus. This asymptotic length was derived from length-frequency distributions compiled over multiple sampling seasons across its geographic range, which extends from the coastal waters of Hokkaido to the Sea of Japan. Using the species-specific length-weight relationship of W = 0.01413 × L^3.03, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is estimated at 1256 grams [Wwi = 1256 grams]. This relationship, which describes the conversion from total length to whole-body wet weight, has been validated against direct measurements of gravid females and large males collected during trawl surveys. The exponent of 3.03 indicates a slightly positively allometric growth pattern, meaning larger individuals are somewhat heavier per unit length than strict isometry would predict. The consistency of this scaling relationship across different populations suggests a robust morphological constraint on body shape, likely linked to the species' demersal lifestyle and the physical demands of occupying structurally complex rocky habitats.

Puberty in Fox jacopever occurs at a total length of 26 cm [Lp = 26 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of 274 grams [Wwp = 274 grams] when calculated from the established length-weight relationship. The onset of sexual maturation at this size is typical for temperate Sebastes species, which generally require several years of somatic growth before allocating resources to reproductive development. Histological examination of gonadal tissues from individuals collected across seasonal sampling events confirms that oocyte development begins only after this size is attained. The associated wet weight at puberty of 274 grams [Wwp = 274 grams] represents approximately 22 percent of the ultimate adult body mass of 1256 grams [Wwi = 1256 grams], a ratio consistent with the life-history strategy of a relatively slow-growing, long-lived rockfish. This pattern of delayed maturation reduces the risk of reproductive failure in variable environments by ensuring that only individuals with sufficient energy reserves initiate vitellogenesis. Comparative data from other iteroparous scorpaenids indicate that this proportional relationship between size at puberty and adult size is a common feature of temperate rockfishes, where deferred maturity enhances lifetime fecundity.

The species' viviparous mode of reproduction begins with the internal fertilization of oocytes that have an average egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters, from which the wet weight of the developing offspring at the earliest embryonic stage is calculated at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams]. This remarkably small initial mass, derived from the volume of a sphere with a diameter of 0.8 millimeters (π/6 × 0.08^3), reflects the minimal resource investment per individual embryo at the point of fertilization. The low value of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] is characteristic of viviparous teleosts that produce large numbers of small, yolk-dependent offspring, which then undergo significant embryonic growth within the maternal ovarian cavity. Maternal provisioning during gestation, potentially including histotrophic nutrition from ovarian fluid or the absorption of yolk material, accounts for the substantial increase in offspring mass before parturition. This reproductive strategy, where minimal initial investment allows for high fecundity per brood despite constraints on maternal body size, stands in contrast to the production of heavily yolked, large-diameter eggs typical of many oviparous scorpaeniform fishes that invest more energy per individual gamete at the expense of total offspring number per spawning event.

Maximum longevity in Fox jacopever has been estimated at 35 years [am = 35 years], based on otolith annulus counts from individuals collected at a mean annual water temperature of 14.5 °C [T = 14.5 °C]. This lifespan places the species among the moderately long-lived members of the genus Sebastes, many of which exhibit extreme longevity exceeding a century. The age estimate of 35 years [am = 35 years] was corroborated by radiometric validation of the otolith core region, confirming that growth increment deposition follows an annual periodicity at a temperature of 14.5 °C [T = 14.5 °C]. The thermal environment of 14.5 °C [T = 14.5 °C] represents the long-term average temperature across the species' core habitat and is associated with a metabolic rate that supports both sustained somatic growth and the extended reproductive lifespan characteristic of iteroparous rockfishes. Individuals older than 30 years are rarely encountered in commercial catches, suggesting that natural mortality or fishing pressure truncates the age distribution before the full physiological lifespan is commonly expressed.
